claims.text: The starting catalyst is a near-equiatomic high-entropy alloy of Cu, Ni, Co, Fe, and a low loading of Pd.
The proposed treatment consists of 3–5 cycles of oxidation at approximately 150 °C for 30 minutes in 1–5% O2, approximately 500 ppm NO, and 2% H2O, followed by annealing at 200 °C in H2 or inert gas.
Post-synthesis oxidation–reduction cycling will induce surface segregation and create a thin surface-modified dual-phase layer on the alloy.
The cycling treatment will form segregated Cu-rich surface domains.
The cycling treatment will form isolated, stabilized Pd sites or small Pd clusters.
Cu-rich domains will enhance low-temperature CO and hydrocarbon oxidation.
Isolated Pd sites will be less prone to poisoning by automotive-exhaust species.
A high-entropy alloy core will anchor the modified surface and provide structural durability.
Selective oxidation of the base metals promotes surface diffusion during the oxidation stage.
Oxidation drives Pd segregation into isolated surface sites.
Cu remains largely metallic during the oxidation stage.
A subsequent reductive anneal can reverse excessive oxidation generated during the oxidation stage.
The reductive anneal locks in the beneficial Cu-rich and isolated-Pd configuration.
The treated catalyst will achieve complete oxidation of CO and hydrocarbons below 150 °C.
The treated catalyst will resist NO-induced deactivation better than the untreated catalyst.
The treated catalyst will resist H2O-induced deactivation better than the untreated catalyst.
The treated catalyst will retain structural integrity and catalytic performance through approximately 1000 hours of cycling.
Compared with the treated catalyst, the untreated catalyst is expected to have poorer low-temperature activity, greater poisoning susceptibility, and a shorter operational lifetime.

contradictions.description: The intervention permits either H2 or an inert gas for the nominally reductive anneal, but the mechanism requires that this step reverse oxidation; an inert atmosphere is not intrinsically reducing.

The predicted outcome requires complete oxidation below 150 °C, whereas the experiment labels T90—the temperature for 90% conversion—as the temperature of complete oxidation. T90 does not directly establish complete conversion.
